cards.name: Number / list headline
cards.summary: Put an exact count in the headline ('7 GST notice replies that...') so the reader knows the size of the payoff and that the piece is skimmable. A good one uses a numeral, picks the number the material actually supports, and every item in the body earns its slot.
use_for: blog and listicle titles
YouTube titles for tips, tools and compilation videos
carousel cover slide ('5 ...' on slide 1, one item per slide)
roundup newsletter subject lines
first line of a LinkedIn post before the 'see more' cut
avoid: Padding to reach a big round number ('101 ways', '50 tools'): count the items you can defend and use that number, even if it is 6.
Using a list title for a piece that is one argument or one method: use hook:how_to or hook:contrarian instead.
Expecting a list post to earn backlinks: Backlinko's 2019 study found list posts strong for shares but weak for links; for a link-earning piece use a 'why' or 'what' research title (hook:reason_why).
Spelling the number out ('Seven ways'): use the numeral (tech:numerals), it is what the eye catches in a feed or search result.
'The 5 best...' with no testing behind the ranking: say how you ranked ('ranked by delivery time in our 30 test orders') or drop 'best'.
templates: [N] [ways / reasons / tools / mistakes] to [result] [qualifier: for whom, by when].
[N] [tools] I use to [result] (and [N] I stopped paying for).
[N] [cheezein] jo har [audience] ko [moment] se pehle pata honi chahiye.
examples: 7 GST notice replies that closed the case in one round, with the exact wording.
5 free tools a 4-person CA office in Jaipur runs on in 2026.
Shaadi se pehle 6 paise ki baatein jo couples skip kar dete hain.
9 Meesho listing fixes, ranked by how fast each one paid off.
cards.why_it_works: The number tells the reader the size of the commitment and promises a structure they can skim, so the click feels low-risk. Backlinko with BuzzSumo (2019, 912 million posts) found list posts got an average of 218% more shares than how-to posts, while the same study found them weak for backlinks. Copyblogger and CoSchedule both name the list headline as a core type, and a listicle title typically states its count (Wikipedia).
cards.risk: Broken promise when the count is inflated (items repeat, the last item is 'follow us for more') or the title says 10 and the body delivers 6 plus filler. Clickbait when a ranked list ('The 5 best...') implies testing that never happened. Legal line: in an ad, 'No. 1', 'best' or a ranked comparison is an objectively factual claim and must be capable of substantiation, with source and date when it rests on research (CCPA 2022 cl. 12, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022; ASCI Code Ch I.1, comp:asci_code). Obvious hyperbole that no one reads literally is allowed.

cards.name: 'You don't have to be X to Y' headline
cards.summary: Name the barrier the reader assumes rules them out (money, expertise, fluent English, a degree, a big team) and remove it: 'You don't have to be [X] to [result]'. A good one picks the barrier from real customer objections and backs the removal in the very next line with the mechanism or the real minimum.
use_for: ads and landing-page heroes for beginner products: tools, templates, courses, first-time services
reel hooks for 'you can do this too' education
webinar and workshop registration headlines
nurture-email subject lines for leads who signed up but never bought
service pitches to small businesses who think agencies are 'for big brands'
avoid: Removing a barrier that is real (you do need some capital, some practice, some time): lower it with the true minimum instead ('Start with Rs 500 and one weekend').
Talking down to the reader ('Even you can...'): state the barrier neutrally and let the mechanism do the reassuring.
Using it on an audience that does not hold the objection (experts, existing customers): use hook:specificity or hook:like_a_pro.
Leaving the 'how' for later: the line after the hook must name what replaces the barrier (a template, a tool, a 3-step method).
templates: You don't have to be [assumed requirement] to [result].
No [barrier]? You can still [result]. Here's how.
[Result] ke liye [barrier] hona zaroori nahi hai.
[Barrier] nahi hai? Koi baat nahi. [Result] aise hoga: [mechanism].
examples: You don't have to be a designer to make a menu card your customers photograph.
Fluent English nahi hai? Interview phir bhi nikal jayega, agar ye 4 answers ready hain.
You don't need a CA on retainer to file your first GST return. You need these 3 documents.
Instagram pe grow karne ke liye dance karna zaroori nahi hai. Ye 3 formats try karo.
cards.why_it_works: An unspoken objection stops action before interest starts; naming the hidden disqualifier and removing it lets the reader see themselves as eligible, which is what makes the rest of the piece feel relevant. Copyblogger lists 'You don't have to be [X] to [Y]' among its 22 headline formulas. The body then has to carry the proof, which is tech:objection_handling.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the body quietly reintroduces the barrier: the 'no money needed' course costs Rs 25,000, the 'no coding' tool needs code. Clickbait territory: 'You don't need money to start trading', 'No degree, Rs 1 lakh a month'. Legal line in India: claims must be capable of substantiation and a disclaimer may clarify but never contradict the headline (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022); coaching and ed-tech ads may not promise guaranteed selection, jobs or salary increases (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024). In Meta ads the barrier must not imply the viewer's personal attribute ('Broke? Still...' implies financial status) (comp:meta_advertising_standards).

cards.name: Price / offer headline
cards.summary: Lead with the deal itself when the price is the news: the exact price, the cut, the EMI, or the free thing. A good one states the real number, what is included, and the condition (date, minimum order) in the same line or the next, so the price in the headline is the price at checkout.
use_for: festive and sale campaigns (Diwali, Navratri, end-of-season sale) in Meta and search ads
promotional email subject lines and WhatsApp broadcast first lines
search ad headlines where the buyer is comparing prices
launch pricing and introductory offers
print, OOH and pamphlet ads for local retail
avoid: Leading on price when the reader does not yet know what the product is: open with the problem or result (hook:problem_solution, hook:before_after) and put the price second.
'Up to 70% off' when most items are 10% off: state the real flat rate or the real range.
'FREE' or 'SALE' in capitals in Google search ads: the editorial policy rejects gimmicky capitalisation; write 'Free delivery'.
Calling something free when delivery, a 'convenience fee' or a subscription follows: say 'free with any order above Rs 999' or drop 'free'.
Price-led headlines for a premium brand whose whole case is quality: lead with the result and let the price sit in the body.
templates: Free [item] with every [purchase] above Rs [threshold], till [date].
Sirf Rs [price] mein [product], [what's included] ke saath.
examples: Hand-block cotton kurtas, Rs 899 each. Same price for every size.
Flat 20% off every planner till Sunday midnight. No code needed.
Free blouse stitching on any saree above Rs 1,500 this Navratri.
Sirf Rs 49 mein poore mahine ka meal plan, shopping list ke saath.
cards.why_it_works: When the reader is already shopping the category, 'how much' is the decision variable; a headline that answers it saves a click and filters out people who could never afford it. Caples' tested headline categories include price and offer headlines (Lofgren's summary). An exact figure also reads as more honest than 'great prices'.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the headline price is not what the buyer pays: fees added at checkout (drip pricing), a 'from Rs 99' item that is out of stock (bait), a 'sale' price that was never higher. Legal line in India: 'free' only when the consumer pays nothing beyond the unavoidable delivery or response cost, no 'free trial' for money-back offers (CCPA 2022 cl. 7); no vague 'up to' or 'as low as' framing for prices, state the fixed price (cl. 12(e)(i)); no bait ads (cl. 5) (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022). Drip pricing, bait and switch and fake time-limited sales are banned dark patterns (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023). Google Ads bans pricing that creates 'a false or misleading impression of the cost' (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation). Promotional SMS must go on a registered DLT template with an opt-out in the same message (comp:trai_tcccpr_2018).

cards.name: Pattern interrupt / visual-verbal mismatch
cards.summary: Break what the viewer expects in the first second (an odd visual, a hard cut, a line that contradicts what is on screen), then land the problem or promise within the next two seconds. The interrupt buys a look; the line after it decides whether they stay, so the oddity should be the product or the problem shown in an unexpected way.
use_for: the first second of reels, Shorts and vertical video ads
UGC and creator ad openers (trend:creator_led_ads)
YouTube pre-roll before the skip button
carousel slide 1 with an image that contradicts its headline
muted autoplay video on LinkedIn or Facebook, carried by on-screen text
avoid: An interrupt unrelated to the message (a scream, a slap, a random explosion): viewers feel tricked and leave at second 3. Make the oddity demonstrate the claim, e.g. a 'leak-proof' bottle thrown onto a sofa.
Sound-only interrupts: much short video is watched muted, so put the twist in the picture and the on-screen text (tech:onscreen_text_vs_vo).
The same interrupt in every post: it stops being unexpected; rotate the type (visual, verbal, edit).
Interrupts with no follow-through line: script the 1-3 second line (problem, product or promise) before you design the shock.
templates: [Visual that contradicts the line] + on-screen text: '[line the visual proves wrong]'.
[Ordinary object] used for the wrong job. Text: 'Ye [object] nahi, [problem] ka solution hai.'
Open mid-[action] on a hard cut; line at 1 s: '[problem or promise in under 8 words]'.
Text: '[what everyone expects]'. Cut to: [the opposite, shown].
Line at 0 s that contradicts what the viewer believes: '[common belief] galat hai.' Then the real point at 2 s: '[what is actually true]'.
examples: Visual: a CA pours a glass of water over a stack of paper invoices. On-screen: 'Paper bills ka yahi hota hai. Scan karo, 2 minute mein.'
Visual: a bride at her mehendi staring at a spreadsheet instead of a mirror. Line: 'Shaadi ka sabse bada kharcha decor nahi tha.'
Visual: a founder deletes his own homepage on camera. Line: 'This page was losing us leads. Here's what replaced it.'
Visual: a steel bottle thrown across the room onto a white sofa, then opened. On-screen: 'Leak-proof ka matlab ye hai.'
cards.why_it_works: A feed trains the eye to expect a familiar first frame; a mismatch makes the viewer look twice before the thumb moves. Zeely's timing for ad openers is 0-1 s pattern break, 1-3 s product, problem or promise, 3-6 s proof (practitioner guidance, not platform data). Insense and TrueFan list visual scroll-stoppers among reel hook types for brands, including India-specific ones.
cards.risk: Clickbait when the interrupt has nothing to do with what follows, or fakes something the viewer must react to: a fake cracked screen, a fake notification, a fake 'breaking news' strap. Legal line: Google Ads bans 'clickbait tactics or sensationalist text or imagery' and ad designs that mimic system notifications (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation). In India, realistic AI-generated footage that makes a person or event look real must carry a prominent label (comp:it_rules_sgi_2026), and from about December 2026 ASCI bans AI result visuals that exaggerate product results even with a label (comp:asci_ai_sgc_labelling).

cards.name: Personal story opener
cards.summary: Open on one specific first-person moment (a date, a place, a mistake, a number) that sets up the lesson: 'How [event] made me [result]', 'I was wrong about...'. A good one starts inside the moment, not with 'Let me tell you a story', and the story is true and belongs to the byline (the writer's or, ghostwritten, the client's).
use_for: founder and executive LinkedIn posts, including ghostwritten ones
newsletter openers
YouTube intros and reel voice-over hooks for personal channels
About pages and brand-story openers
speech, webinar and podcast openings
avoid: Preambles ('Story time', 'Let me tell you something'): start at the moment ('Tuesday, 11:40 pm, the GST portal logged me out').
A story with no lesson for the reader: tie the last line of the moment to the reader's problem, or cut the story.
Inventing an anecdote for a ghostwritten post: interview the client for a real one (tech:sme_interview) and get sign-off on every fact.
The humblebrag 'mistake' that is really a flex ('My biggest mistake was working too hard'): pick a mistake that cost something.
templates: How [specific event] made me [result / changed belief].
I was wrong about [belief]. [The moment that proved it].
[N] years ago I [mistake]. Today [result]. Here's what changed.
Us din [jagah] mein [person] ne kaha '[line]'. Tab samajh aaya [lesson].
examples: In 2019 I lost my biggest client over one WhatsApp message. Here's what I'd send instead.
Papa ki dukaan pe pehla UPI QR maine lagaya tha. Teen mahine mein galla khaali rehne laga.
How a Rs 300 courier mistake made our Surat store rewrite its returns page.
I was wrong about cold email. Forty sends, zero replies, then I changed one line.
cards.why_it_works: A concrete first-person moment signals real experience and gives the reader a character to follow, and it opens a loop: what happened next? Copyblogger lists the 'How [event] made me [result]' story headline among its 22 formulas, and a narrative hook is by definition the opening that makes the reader keep going (Wikipedia). The best-known story headline in direct response is Caples' own 'They Laughed When I Sat Down At the Piano' ad.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the 'story' is an invented parable or a pitch in disguise that never returns to the lesson. Legal line: if the story sells something the storyteller is paid for, gets free, or earns commission on, disclose the material connection up front, not at the end (comp:asci_influencer, comp:endorsement_know_hows). A result inside a story used in an ad ('I cleared my loan in 8 months with this app') is a claim that must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022).

cards.name: Personalised subject line
cards.summary: Insert a recipient-specific detail (first name, city, the item they saved, the event they attended) through merge tags so the subject reads as written for them. A good one uses a detail that changes the meaning of the line (their order status, their city's date), not a name bolted onto a generic offer, and every merge field has a fallback.
use_for: lifecycle email: abandoned cart, back-in-stock, renewal, refund and delivery updates
event follow-ups ('Priya, your workshop notes')
segmented newsletters by city or interest
cold outreach that names the company or a specific observation
push notifications and WhatsApp templates with variables
avoid: Empty or broken merge fields ('Hi ,', 'Hi {FNAME}', 'Hi PRIYA SHARMA'): set a fallback ('there', the city name) and normalise case in the CRM before sending.
Using data the person did not knowingly give or would find creepy ('Still thinking about that pregnancy test?'): personalise only with declared or transactional data.
Name-only personalisation on a mass promo: a detail tied to their action (the size they saved) does more than their name.
Personalising a bought or scraped list: wrong names and no consent; build the list yourself.
templates: [First name], your [product / order] [status or next step].
[First name], the [item they saved] is back in [size / colour].
examples: Priya, your Rs 1,240 refund is on its way
Ananya, the size M kurta you saved is back
Indore workshop Sunday ko: venue badal gaya hai
For Sharma Textiles: 3 RTO fixes from your last 50 orders
cards.why_it_works: People scan an inbox for 'this is for me'; their own name, city or recent action is the strongest match. Mailchimp's guidance: use merge tags for name or location, personalisation 'is shown to increase open rates for most users', and keep subject lines to no more than 9 words and 60 characters.
cards.risk: Tips into deception when the personal touch fakes a relationship ('Rohit, following up on our call' when there was no call) or a fake 'Re:'. Legal line: US commercial email must not use misleading headers and 'The subject line must accurately reflect the content of the message' (comp:can_spam). India's DPDP Act needs specific, purpose-stated consent to use personal data for marketing; the Rules were notified on 14 Nov 2025 with phased compliance (comp:dpdp_act_rules). UK and EU individuals need consent or the soft opt-in (comp:uk_pecr, comp:gdpr_marketing_consent). For India SMS, the body must match a registered DLT template; TRAI's 2025 note says at least 30% of a template stays fixed and more than three variables needs justification (comp:trai_tcccpr_2018).

cards.name: POV hook
cards.summary: 'POV: you [are in a specific situation]' puts the viewer inside a scene they recognise before any product appears. A good POV is hyper-specific (time, place, one telling detail), the camera actually plays the viewer's eyes, and the product arrives as the natural next beat of the scene, not as a cutaway pitch.
use_for: organic reels and Shorts for D2C and service brands
UGC and creator ad openers
relatable-comedy posts and meme captions
on-screen text over b-roll when there is no voice-over
Threads and X posts written as a one-line scene
avoid: Generic POVs ('POV: you love coffee'): add the situation and the stake ('POV: 8:55 am, standup at 9, and the geyser just died').
POV text over footage that is not from the viewer's eyes (a third-person shot of the creator talking): either shoot first-person or use hook:audience_callout.
POV in formats where the convention is not native (search ads, formal email, B2B proposals): use hook:you_direct_address.
A POV scene with no payoff (the joke never lands, the product never fits the scene): script the last beat first.
templates: POV: it's [date / season] and you still haven't [task].
examples: POV: it's 31 July, 11:52 pm, and the income tax portal just logged you out.
POV: shaadi ka card aa gaya hai aur tumhare paas 'pehenne ko kuch nahi hai'.
POV: you run a cloud kitchen and the third 'food was cold' review of the week just came in.
POV: mummy ne guests ke saamne bola, 'beta, zara wifi theek kar do'.
cards.why_it_works: It starts with identity, not features (Zeely): the viewer recognises their own moment and stays to see how it resolves. TrueFan lists POV among the trending India hook formats of 2026, and Insense includes POV openers in its reel hook templates for brands.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the POV sets up a relatable moment and then cuts to a hard sell that ignores the scene. Clickbait when the scene is fake drama unrelated to the product ('POV: you just got arrested' for a phone case). Legal line: in Meta ads a POV that names the viewer's condition ('POV: you're diabetic and...') implies a personal attribute and is disallowed (comp:meta_advertising_standards); a creator performing a brand's POV needs an upfront ad label (comp:asci_influencer).

cards.name: Problem-solved headline
cards.summary: Name one specific, felt problem and promise it ends: 'Get rid of [problem] once and for all'. A good one names the problem in the reader's own words (from reviews, DMs, calls), hints at the mechanism, and promises no more than the product can prove.
use_for: ad headlines and reel hooks for products that fix one clear annoyance
landing-page heroes for single-problem services
nurture-email subject lines that introduce the fix
how-to blog and YouTube titles
the first bullet of a marketplace listing
avoid: 'Once and for all', 'forever', 'permanently' when the fix is partial: say what it really does ('cut the calls by half', 'stop it this monsoon').
Vague problems ('Struggling with growth?'): lift the exact phrase customers use (tech:voice_of_customer_mining), e.g. 'kab tak aayega?' calls.
Health, skin, hair and disease 'get rid of' lines: these are cure claims; describe the product and its tested benefit instead.
Leading with a problem the audience does not know they have: use a story or hook:curiosity_gap to make them aware first.
templates: Get rid of [problem] [time qualifier], without [unwanted cost].  (for annoyances you remove, not things you repair)
[Audience] stuck with [problem]? [Mechanism] that worked for [named case].
examples: Get rid of the 'kab tak aayega?' calls: send tracking on WhatsApp automatically.
Almirah mein seelan ki smell? Is monsoon ye 2 cheezein rakh ke dekho.
Stop chasing clients for payment: add this one line to every invoice.
No more double-booked slots at your salon: one shared calendar, set up in 20 minutes.
cards.why_it_works: A named problem filters for the people who have it and promises relief in the same breath. Copyblogger lists 'Get rid of [problem] once and for all' among its 22 formulas, and CreatorsJet frames reel hooks as jobs that include calling out a mistake and promising a payoff. The full-piece structure is fw:pas.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the headline says 'once and for all' and the body says 'reduce', or the fix needs a paid upgrade the headline hid. Legal line: claims must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:asci_code). Drug or remedy ads that suggest cure, treatment or prevention of scheduled diseases are barred by the DMR Act, and 'taking part in the publication' covers the writer (comp:dmr_act_1954). Meta bans claims to 'cure, heal, or eliminate' a listed set of conditions such as diabetes, thyroid and psoriasis (comp:meta_advertising_standards). Google bans presenting an improbable result as the likely outcome (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation).

cards.name: Question headline
cards.summary: Ask the question the reader is already asking (often the exact search query), or one they cannot answer without reading. A good question is specific, has a non-obvious answer the piece actually gives, and cannot be dismissed with a quick 'no'.
use_for: blog and YouTube titles that match a search query ('Is term insurance worth it at 25?')
FAQ and answer articles written to be cited by AI search
first line of a LinkedIn, X or Threads post
quiz-style reel openers
newsletter subject lines when the answer is the body
avoid: Yes/no questions the reader answers 'no' to and leaves ('Want more sales?'): ask which, why, how much or what happens if.
Questions the body answers with 'it depends' and nothing else: give a default answer and the conditions that change it.
Asking about the viewer's condition in a Meta ad ('In debt?', 'Depression getting you down?'): Meta disallows both styles; ask about the product or situation instead.
A question headline on a news story whose answer is unknown ('Was it sabotage?'): report what is known with hook:news_announcement.
templates: [Option A] or [Option B]: which one [outcome] for [audience]?
How much does [thing] actually cost in [city]?
[Situation] mein kya karein: [option A] ya [option B]?
examples: Is a Rs 1 crore term plan enough for a family of four in Pune?
Why does your sourdough go flat on humid Mumbai days?
Home loan prepay karein ya SIP badhayein? Dono ka hisaab ek sheet mein.
Composition or regular GST: which one saves more for a Rs 40 lakh cafe?
cards.why_it_works: A question opens a gap the reader wants closed and mirrors the words people type into search and AI assistants. Backlinko's 2019 study of 912 million posts found titles ending in '?' got 23.3% more social shares than those that did not. CoSchedule names the question headline as a core blog type, and Caples' tested categories include it (Lofgren's summary).
cards.risk: Clickbait when the question implies something untrue ('Is your phone spying on you?' to sell a phone cover) or the body never answers it. A question about a named person ('Did [leader] take a bribe?') is still an imputation: defamation under BNS s.356 covers spoken, written or visual imputations, and the exceptions protect good-faith opinion on public conduct, not invented insinuation (comp:bns_defamation_speech). Meta's own disallowed ad example is 'Are you bankrupt? Check out our services.' (comp:meta_advertising_standards).

cards.name: Quick and easy headline
cards.summary: Promise the result for less time or effort than the reader expects: 'Here's a quick way to...', 'The lazy person's way to...'. A good one quantifies the effort honestly ('10 minutes once, then automatic') and the body proves it with steps short enough to match the claim.
use_for: tutorial reels and how-to Shorts
template, checklist and tool lead magnets
recipe titles and food reels
product demos for simple apps and tools
Pinterest pins and blog titles for hacks
avoid: Calling a hard job easy (tax notices, weight loss, visa paperwork): say how long it took and for whom ('took me 40 minutes the first time').
Stacking 'quick, easy, simple' in one line: pick one and put a number on it.
'Lazy' framing for a formal B2B or finance audience: use 'in one meeting' or 'without a new tool'.
Speed promises on high-stakes decisions (insurance, investing, medical): fast reads as careless; lead with clarity, not speed.

Done-for-you products (delivery, a service that does the task): do not quantify the ordering ([N] taps, 3 steps: pick, order, eat), which was never the hassle; size the effort the reader skips (the hour of cooking, Sunday meal-prep, the tiffin to pack) or name the hassle removed.
templates: [Result] in [N] minutes, using only [tool you already have].
Here's a quick way to [task] without [usual hassle].
examples: The lazy way to plan a week of tiffins: one Sunday list, seven dinners.
Rent receipt sirf 2 minute mein, bina kisi app ke.
A quick way to see which product actually makes you money: one extra Excel column.
Pressure-cooker biryani in 30 minutes. No dum, no oven.
cards.why_it_works: Effort and time are part of the price the reader pays; shrinking them raises the value of the same result (the time and effort terms of fw:hormozi_value_equation). Copyblogger lists 'Here's a quick way to [solve a problem]', and Caples' benefit headlines include quick-and-easy promises (Lofgren's summary).
cards.risk: Broken promise when the 'quick' method needs paid tools, prior skill or hidden steps, or the '5-minute' video runs 18 minutes before the method. Clickbait: 'easy money', 'earn from your phone in 10 minutes'. Legal line: claims must be capable of substantiation and a disclaimer may not contradict the headline (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022); Meta bans promises of specific outcomes within a set timeframe without qualifiers in health and weight-loss ads (comp:meta_advertising_standards); Google bans presenting an improbable result as the likely outcome (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation).

cards.name: Plain-text 'quick question' subject line
cards.summary: A short, lower-case, colleague-style subject line ('quick question about sharma textiles', 'gst notice q') for one-to-one cold outreach. It works when the email it opens is genuinely short and asks one real question about the recipient's business, and fails when it hides a long pitch.
use_for: B2B cold email to one named person
partnership, podcast-guest and media pitches
follow-ups after a warm introduction
founder-to-customer plain-text emails asking for feedback
avoid: Bulk newsletters and promotions: a colleague-style subject on a campaign email reads as a trick; use hook:descriptive_subject_line.
A bare 'quick question' with nothing specific: add the company, the topic or the mutual contact ('quick question about your diwali catalogue').
A fake 'Re:' or 'Fwd:', or 'following up on our call' when there was no call: it implies a thread that does not exist.
Sales words in the subject ('demo', 'offer', 'free'): Gong's cold-email data, as reported by 30 Minutes to President's Club, found salesy techniques cut opens by as much as 17.9%.
A 300-word body under a 'quick' subject: keep the body to a few lines and one question the recipient can answer in one reply.
examples: quick question about sharma textiles' returns
idea for your diwali catalogue
gst notice q for patel & co
aapki google listing ke baare mein
cards.why_it_works: Short lower-case subjects look like a note from a colleague, not a campaign, so they get opened as conversation rather than filtered as marketing. 30 Minutes to President's Club, reporting Gong data on 85M+ cold emails: all-lowercase subject lines had the highest open rates, 1-4 words is the ideal range, and salesy techniques reduced open rates by as much as 17.9%. These are vendor-reported figures (confidence low): treat them as direction, and test on your own list.
cards.risk: Tips into deception when the subject implies a relationship or prior thread that does not exist, or when 'quick question' opens a pitch with no question in it. Legal line: under CAN-SPAM, header information must not be misleading and 'The subject line must accurately reflect the content of the message' (comp:can_spam). Cold email to individuals in the UK needs specific consent or the soft opt-in, and the sender must not disguise their identity (comp:uk_pecr). High complaint rates also get bulk cold email filtered by Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook (trend:email_deliverability_rules).

cards.name: Reason-why headline
cards.summary: Promise an explanation: '[N] reasons why...' or 'Why [surprising fact]'. A good one picks a 'why' the reader has actually wondered about and delivers real causes (data, mechanism, named sources), not opinions dressed as reasons.
use_for: explainer blog posts and YouTube explainers
news explainers once the causes are known
B2B thought-leadership and research-post titles meant to earn links
reasons-to-buy sections and sales-page subheads
reel hooks in the 'isliye...' form (see hook:this_is_why for the spoken opener)
avoid: 'Why' headlines that explain nothing new ('Why marketing matters'): make the why specific or surprising ('Why your Google reviews dry up after month one').
Padding a reasons list with weak reasons: three strong reasons beat seven with filler.
'Why X happened' on breaking news before causes are confirmed: use 'what we know' framing (hook:news_announcement) and attribute every cause.
A 'reasons to buy' headline whose reasons are features: turn each into what it does for the buyer (tech:features_to_benefits).
templates: Why [surprising fact] (and what it means for [audience]).
examples: Why sabzi prices jump every monsoon, explained with mandi arrival data.
4 reasons Surat textile traders are moving their catalogues to WhatsApp.
Why your Google reviews dry up after the first month.
Startup ki pehli hiring galat kyun hoti hai: 3 wajah.
cards.why_it_works: A 'why' promises understanding, which people seek out and share, and it signals the piece has substance beyond tips. Caples' keyword openers include 'Why' and 'Because' (Lofgren's summary). Backlinko's 2019 study found 'Why' posts, 'What' posts and infographics got 25.8% more links than videos and how-to posts, which makes this the title to reach for when a piece must earn backlinks. Hopkins' reason-why copy is the full-piece version (fw:reason_why_copy).
cards.risk: Broken promise when the 'reasons' are speculation presented as cause, or the 'why' asserts a fact that is not true. In news, 'Why [official] resigned' needs a confirmed, attributed reason. In ads, reasons that are factual claims ('fastest', 'most trusted', 'No. 1 in Jaipur') must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:asci_code).

cards.name: Secret / insider reveal
cards.summary: Promise insider knowledge: 'The secret of [result]', 'Little-known ways to...', 'What everybody ought to know about...'. It works only when the payload is a real, specific nuance most of the audience does not know, delivered early, ideally from someone with first-hand experience.
use_for: expert reels and carousels from practitioners (a chef, a CA, a property lawyer)
newsletter subject lines that carry one genuine insider tip
YouTube titles for craft and trade knowledge
long-form sales letters that name a unique mechanism
B2B posts sharing an internal process
avoid: Fake secrets (common advice relabelled): Insense and CreatorsJet both warn the hook must share a real nuance. Test: would a working professional in the field nod, or roll their eyes?
'What doctors / banks don't want you to know': conspiracy framing that invites regulatory trouble; say 'the step most people skip'.
Withholding the secret for a 'part 2' or a paid course: deliver it in the piece, sell the depth.
Using 'secret' when the reveal is your product: name the mechanism (tech:unique_mechanism) and show it.
templates: The secret of [result] isn't [assumed cause]. It's [actual cause].
What every [audience] ought to know about [topic] before [moment].
examples: What every first-time Pune flat buyer ought to know about the carpet-area clause.
Halwai ka secret: besan pehle sukha bhuno, ghee baad mein.
The detail a property lawyer checks first in any sale deed: the chain of title, not the price.
Little-known ways tier-2 CA firms win referral clients.
cards.why_it_works: Curiosity plus status: the reader gets to know something others do not. Copyblogger's 22 formulas include 'The secret of [result]', 'Little-known ways to...' and 'What everybody ought to know about...'. TrueFan's 2026 India hook formats include the 'secret app' type, and Insense lists insider-tip hooks for brands while warning it must share a real nuance, not a fake secret.
cards.risk: Clickbait when the 'secret' is common knowledge or held back until a paid product. Broken promise in sales letters that tease a 'secret method' and never name it. Legal line: health 'secret cure' and remedy claims fall under the DMR Act (comp:dmr_act_1954) and Meta's cure-claim ban (comp:meta_advertising_standards); 'secret stock' or return claims by a creator a SEBI-regulated brand pays or refers to are a prohibited association unless the creator is registered (comp:sebi_finfluencer_association); Google Ads bans 'clickbait tactics or sensationalist text' (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation).

cards.name: Shocking statistic
cards.summary: Open with one surprising, sourced number that reframes the topic. A good one names the source and year, keeps the base visible (61% of whom?), translates the number into human scale, and puts the source on screen or in the next line.
use_for: news and policy explainers, reels on civic and money topics
LinkedIn thought-leadership openers
report, survey and white-paper launch posts
PSA scripts and campaign openers
pitch-deck and sales-deck title slides
avoid: The invented '99% log ye galti karte hain': use the real figure with its source, or drop the number and use hook:mistake_warning.
Numbers without base or year ('300% growth'): add 'from 2 to 8 stores' or the survey size and date.
Old stats presented as current: give the year in the line; replace anything older than the topic's change cycle.
Mixing up per cent and percentage points, or crore and million: check the unit against the source before posting.
templates: Only [N] in [M] [group] [action]. [What it means for you].
[Number] [group] [fact]. Source: [source, year]. Ab sawaal ye hai: [question].
examples: 61% of Indian internet users watched short video in 2025 (IAMAI-Kantar). Your brochure isn't in that feed.
YouTube Shorts ab roz average 200 billion views karta hai (YouTube CEO letter, 2026). Aapka product demo kahan hai?
53% of consumers distrust AI search summaries (Gartner 2025 survey, via Fortune). So why does your FAQ read like one?
cards.why_it_works: A concrete, unexpected number breaks an assumption faster than an argument and lends authority to everything after it. Caples' tested headlines include facts-and-figures headlines (Lofgren's summary), and TrueFan lists the shock stat among India's trending hook formats in 2026. The surprise only works if the number is believable and checkable, which is why the source belongs in the hook.
cards.risk: Clickbait when the number is invented, outdated, cherry-picked or stripped of its base (300% growth from 2 users to 8). Legal line: a statistic in an ad is an objectively factual claim and must be capable of substantiation, with the source and date cited when it rests on research (CCPA 2022 cl. 12(a)-(b), comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022; ASCI Code Ch I.1, comp:asci_code). Health statistics in ads also meet Meta's health rules and the DMR Act (comp:meta_advertising_standards, comp:dmr_act_1954).

cards.name: One-to-three-word headline
cards.summary: A headline of one to three words that a strong visual, a subhead or the product itself completes. A good one is half a thought on its own and obvious the moment you see the image, and the subhead underneath carries the specific promise, place or price.
use_for: billboards, hoardings and transit ads read in two seconds
print ads and packaging fronts
carousel cover slides and reel covers with a strong image
short headlines in display and responsive ads
campaign lines that sit above a longer explanatory subhead
avoid: Search ads, SEO titles and email subject lines, where the words must carry the meaning without a picture: use hook:keyword_front_loaded or hook:descriptive_subject_line.
Abstract virtue words ('Quality. Trust. Service.'): use a concrete noun or verb the image proves ('Zero paperwork.').
Publishing the short line without its subhead or visual: test it by covering the image; if the line plus subhead says nothing specific, rewrite the subhead.
English wordplay for a Hindi-belt audience that will not catch the pun: use a Hindi word with the same punch ('Bas.', 'Garam. Abhi.').

Responsive display ads: Google may show a short headline without the description, and the long headline is a separate asset, so a one-word line cannot rely on a subhead (support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7005917); use hook:keyword_front_loaded there.
templates: [One concrete noun].  Subhead: [specific promise, place, price].
[Verb] [object].  Subhead: [who it is for and how].
[Hindi word or phrase].  Subhead: [what to do, where].
examples: Garam. Abhi.  Subhead: Samosas delivered hot in Kothrud, under 20 minutes.
Zero paperwork.  Subhead: GST filing for Jaipur shops, done on WhatsApp.
Bas.  Subhead: Tapakta nal band karo. Har boond ka bill aata hai.
Monday, sorted.  Subhead: 5 lunches prepped in one Sunday hour.
cards.why_it_works: A one-to-three-word line is read in a glance, which is all a hoarding, a thumbnail or a feed cover gets; the visual does the rest of the sentence, and the gap between them makes the viewer finish it. Caples' tested headline categories include one-to-three-word headlines (Lofgren's summary). The classic model is DDB's 'Think small.' for Volkswagen, where the image of a tiny car completes the line.
cards.risk: Rarely clickbait; the failure is ambiguity, or an image-plus-word pair that implies a claim the product cannot back ('Cured.' over a supplement bottle, 'Guaranteed.' over a coaching batch). The word and the visual together are the claim, so it must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:asci_code). In Google ads, gimmicky capitals or symbols ('FREE!!!') are rejected under the editorial policy (comp:google_ads_editorial).

cards.name: Social proof headline
cards.summary: Lead with how many people like the reader use or approve it: 'Here is a method that is helping [group] to [result]', '2,300 Jaipur shopkeepers file GST with us'. A good one uses a verifiable count with its unit and time window, names the peer group the reader belongs to, and never rounds up.
use_for: ad headlines and landing-page heroes for products with real traction
app store and Play Store first lines
B2B trust lines ('used by 40 CA firms in Rajasthan')
launch and waitlist emails
WhatsApp broadcasts to a local audience
avoid: Vanity numbers (impressions, followers, 'views'): use users, orders, repeat buyers or clients, with a time window.
A crowd the reader does not identify with ('Delhi's favourite' to a Chennai audience): name their peer group or city.
Rounding up ('10,000+' when the count is 7,800): use the real number; '7,800' reads as more honest anyway.
Live counters and 'X people are viewing this' widgets unless the number is real and live.
Only one case to point to (one village, one client): that is a story or testimonial, not a crowd; use hook:testimonial or hook:personal_story, or a contrast line.
templates: Here's a method that is helping [group] [result].
[City] ke [number] [group] ye already use kar rahe hain.
examples: 2,300 Jaipur shopkeepers now file GST on WhatsApp with us. Here's how it works.
Here's the 15-minute routine helping first-year B.Com students in Patna pass accounts.
Indore ke 400 gharon mein ab subah ka doodh 7 baje se pehle aata hai.
Used by 40 CA firms across Rajasthan to track every GST notice.
cards.why_it_works: Under uncertainty people copy what similar others do (social proof, the term popularised by Robert Cialdini, per Wikipedia). Copyblogger's formulas include 'Here is a method that is helping [X] to [Y]', and TrueFan lists crowd-proof hooks among India's reel archetypes. The closer the group is to the reader, the stronger the pull.
cards.risk: Fabrication is the line: invented, inflated or bought numbers. Legal line in India: fake popularity is a banned dark pattern, and the gazette's own illustration is 'Only 2 rooms left! 30 others are looking at this right now' (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023); a usage count in an ad must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022). US: the FTC rule bans buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence such as bot followers or views (comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule). UK: fake or concealed-incentive reviews are banned outright (comp:uk_dmcc_schedule20).

cards.name: Specificity headline
cards.summary: Replace every vague word in the headline with the exact number, name, place, timeframe and result ('Rs 2.4 lakh recovered in 41 days' instead of 'big savings, fast'), so the claim reads as measured, not guessed. A good one is true down to the digit and the body shows where each number came from.
use_for: case-study titles and portfolio headlines
B2B ads and LinkedIn posts
landing-page heroes and proof bars
email subject lines for results-led nurture emails
YouTube titles for experiments and breakdowns
avoid: Specific-sounding invented figures: a made-up exact number is a worse lie than a vague one. Get the client's real data or write the headline without the number.
Fake precision ('97.38% faster') unless it is an actual measurement: round to what the reader needs.
Four numbers in one line: keep one or two, move the rest to the body.
A number with no base or window ('300% growth'): add 'from 12 to 48 orders a day, March to June'.
templates: How [named client or type] [result with number] in [timeframe].
examples: How a Jaipur CA firm cut notice replies from 6 days to 2 with one shared tracker.
Rs 2.4 lakh in stuck GST refunds recovered for 11 Surat traders in 41 days.
38 din, hafte mein 3 reels: ek Lucknow bakery ke DMs mein kya badla.
The 9-word subject line that booked 14 calls from 212 cold emails.
cards.why_it_works: Exact figures signal that someone measured, which makes the claim believable and the reader able to picture their own result. 'Ultra-specific' is one of Michael Masterson's 4 Us of a headline (fw:four_us), and Caples lists facts and figures among benefit headlines (Lofgren's summary).
cards.risk: The danger flips here: a false specific number is a stronger, more checkable lie, and a best-ever result presented as typical is a broken promise. Legal line: factual claims must be capable of substantiation, with source and date for research-based ones (CCPA 2022 cl. 12, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022); results quoted from customers must be genuine endorsements (cl. 13-14). Coaching and ed-tech results need the topper's rank, course name and duration, and whether the course was paid, plus written consent (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024).

cards.name: High-stakes YouTube title (MrBeast-style)
cards.summary: A YouTube title that states an extreme, concrete stake or challenge the thumbnail shows at a glance ('I Lived on Rs 100 a Day in Mumbai for a Week'). A good one is decided before filming, the stake is real and on camera, and the first minute proves the title's promise is being kept.
use_for: YouTube challenge, experiment and stunt videos
food, travel and money creators' long-form titles
brand-funded stunts and creator collaborations
Shorts series built on a repeated challenge
pitch titles when planning a video before production
avoid: A stake the video does not deliver (the 'Rs 1 lakh' prize that never appears on screen): film the stake or change the title.
Copying MrBeast-scale stakes without the budget: scale the stake to what you can show ('Rs 50 vs Rs 5,000 thali' is a stake).
Stakes titles on educational or B2B channels where viewers search for answers: use hook:keyword_front_loaded or hook:how_to.
Dangerous stunts, minors at risk, or wasting food for spectacle: the backlash costs more than the views.
templates: I [did extreme thing] for [N days / hours].
I Tried [thing] With Only Rs [small amount].
examples: I Lived on Rs 100 a Day in Mumbai for a Week

I Built a Website for My Mom's Tiffin Service in 24 Hours
Last Person to Leave the Dhaba Wins Rs 10,000

cards.name: 'Stop scrolling' call
cards.summary: Tell the viewer to stop ('Ruko!', 'Don't swipe if you...') and in the same breath give a specific reason that applies to them. The command alone is noise and now overused; the reason (who it is for, what they lose or gain in the next seconds) does all the work.
use_for: reel and Short openers for time-sensitive information: a deadline, a scam alert, a recall
local civic and news alerts for one city or community
festival and sale reminders where the date is real
creator PSAs on money and consumer safety
avoid: The bare 'Stop scrolling!': Insense lists it among weak, overused openers. Lead with the reason itself ('GST notice aaya hai? Reply bhejne se pehle 10 second ruko').
Using it on low-stakes content (a recipe, a vlog): show the result instead (hook:before_after).
Fake alarm ('Ruko! Ye dekh ke shock ho jaoge'): if nothing in the video is urgent, use a curiosity or story hook.
Using it in every post: the viewer learns to ignore it; keep it for genuinely urgent posts.
templates: Don't swipe if you [specific situation]: [what you'll lose or get].
Wait, [city / group] walon: [news or warning in under 10 words].
examples: Ruko, Jaipur ke shop owners: GST notice aaya hai toh reply bhejne se pehle ye dekh lo.
Stop. Before you pay that 'electricity bill pending' SMS, read the sender ID.
Don't swipe if you booked a Goa trip from a Rs 999 Instagram ad. Check this first.
Ruko! Shaadi ka gold book karne se pehle hallmark ka ye number check karo.
cards.why_it_works: A direct command breaks autopilot for a split second; the specific reason that follows tells the viewer it is about them, which is what actually keeps them. Insense says the generic version is weak and overused and works only with a specific reason attached; ebookwaala and TrueFan list the Hindi and Hinglish 'ruko' forms among India reel hooks.
cards.risk: Clickbait when the 'reason' is fake alarm or the urgent tone fronts a routine promo. Legal line: false urgency is a banned dark pattern in India (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023); Google Ads bans using 'negative life events such as death, accidents, illness, arrests or bankruptcy' to pressure immediate action (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation). A promo dressed as an official alert that uses government names or emblems in trade runs into the Emblems and Names Act (comp:emblems_names_act_1950).

cards.name: Testimonial headline
cards.summary: Put a real customer's own words, in quotes and with their name and context, in the headline slot. A good one quotes a specific outcome or moment in the customer's own voice (Hinglish included), trims without rewriting, and has the customer's written permission.
use_for: static and video ads, especially for local services
landing-page heroes and pricing-page headers
case-study titles and testimonial pages
email subject lines for proof emails in a sequence
print ads and brochures
avoid: Invented or 'composite' quotes: every quote must be a real customer's words. The examples on this card show the format only.
Polishing the quote into brand voice: keep the customer's words and grammar, trim for length, never add claims.
Anonymous attribution ('A happy customer'): use name plus role or city, with permission; first name and city if they prefer.
Quotes that claim results the brand itself could not substantiate ('cured my sugar'): drop them, the endorser's words count as the brand's claim.

cards.why_it_works: Words from a third party carry more belief than the brand's own claim, and a real person's phrasing sounds like the reader's own thoughts. cards.name: 'This is why...' explainer hook
cards.summary: Open on the answer to a frustration the viewer has felt but never asked out loud: 'This is why your [X] keeps [problem]'. A good one names a precise, recognisable symptom, gives the cause within the next few seconds, and ends with the fix.
use_for: explainer reels and Shorts for home, kitchen, tech, money and small-business problems
expert creators (a CA, an electrician, a chef) answering common complaints
LinkedIn video and carousel slide 1
Shorts series built on one recurring problem type
ad openers for a product that removes a known cause
avoid: Broad symptoms ('This is why you're not successful'): name an observable one ('why your shop gets calls but no walk-ins').
A 'cause' that is opinion or a generational jab ('This is why Gen Z can't focus'): if you cannot point to the mechanism, use hook:contrarian and own it as a view.
Holding the cause until the end: give it early and spend the rest on the fix, or viewers feel baited.
Medical 'this is why you have [condition]' lines: that is diagnosis; point to a doctor and keep product claims out.
templates: This is why [audience] [observed behaviour], and the fix.
That's why [common belief] is wrong: [cause in one line].
examples: This is why your shop gets Google calls but no walk-ins: the map pin is 300 metres off.
Isliye aapke WhatsApp broadcast ka reply nahi aata: pehli line sirf 'Dear customer' hai.
This is why your new phone dies by 4 pm: three apps you never open.

cards.why_it_works: It promises closure on a frustration the viewer already has, so the payoff feels personal and immediate. Zeely lists 'this is why' among native ad openers and TrueFan includes the form in India reel archetypes. It is the spoken, short-form cousin of hook:reason_why and runs on tech:open_loop.

cards.summary: Thumbnail text and title do different jobs: the image text adds two to four words of stake, emotion or number that the title does not repeat, and the title explains with the important words first. Together they promise exactly what the video delivers.
use_for: YouTube long-form titles and thumbnails

podcast episode artwork and titles
Pinterest pin image text and pin title
course and webinar thumbnails
avoid: Repeating the title word for word on the thumbnail: use the image for what the title cannot say in the same glance (the stake, the reaction, the number).
ALL CAPS and emoji everywhere: YouTube Help advises limiting both; keep caps for one word if any.
Thumbnail text too long to read on a phone: two to four words, high contrast, clear of faces.
Burying the key word at the end of a long title: put the important words first, as YouTube Help advises.
A thumbnail or title promising something the video does not contain: change the packaging, not the viewer's expectation.

Thumbnail: '[before] vs [after]' | Title: 'How [subject] went from [before] to [after]'

cards.name: Time-bound promise ('Give me X, I'll give you Y')
cards.summary: Trade a small, fixed amount of the reader's time for one concrete result: 'Give me [5 minutes] and I'll give you [result]'. A good one keeps the time honest (the piece really takes that long) and the result is a single thing the reader can do or has in hand afterwards.
use_for: YouTube intros and podcast cold opens
webinar and workshop invitations
newsletter openers and lead-magnet titles
mini-tutorial reels ('60 second do...')
LinkedIn posts that teach one skill
avoid: A time claim the content breaks (a 20-minute video promising 5): match the number to the runtime or reading time.
Promising a transformation in the time slot ('Give me 10 minutes, I'll make you rich'): promise an output (a template, a fixed headline, a checklist).
Vague results ('a better business'): name the artefact the reader leaves with.
Timed outcomes in health, fitness and weight-loss ads: Meta bans specific outcomes within a set timeframe without qualifiers.
templates: Give me [N minutes] and I'll [show / give] you [specific result].

examples: Give me 7 minutes and you'll have a GST invoice template your CA won't need to fix.

cards.why_it_works: A bounded time cost lowers the commitment while the named output raises the value, the time and effort terms of fw:hormozi_value_equation. Copyblogger lists 'Give me [short time] and I'll give you [result]' among its 22 formulas.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the result needs more time than promised or a purchase the hook hid. Legal line: claims must be capable of substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022); coaching ads may not promise guaranteed selection, ranks or jobs (comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024); Meta bans 'promises of specific outcomes within a set timeframe without disclaimers or qualifiers' in health ads (comp:meta_advertising_standards).

cards.name: Ultimate / complete guide title
cards.summary: 'The [complete / ultimate] guide to [topic] ([year])' promises one page that covers everything a searcher needs. It holds only when the page genuinely covers the topic end to end, the year in the title is true (content updated), and the page is organised so readers can jump to their part.
use_for: pillar pages and long-form SEO articles
ebooks and gated guides
long YouTube tutorials with chapters
B2B playbooks
KDP non-fiction subtitles
avoid: 'Ultimate guide' on a 900-word post: call it what it is ('quick guide', 'checklist').
A stale year in the title: update the content and the year together, or drop the year.
'Ultimate' when a specific scope says more: 'Every GST form a Jaipur cafe files, with due dates' beats 'The ultimate GST guide'.
Mass-producing 'ultimate guides' with AI for rankings: that is the pattern Google's scaled content abuse policy targets; publish fewer, deeper pages.
templates: Everything [audience] needs to know about [topic] in [year].
examples: The complete guide to GST for home bakers in 2026, with filled sample invoices
Pune rental agreements: the complete tenant's guide, from token amount to move-out
Shaadi ke liye passport, visa aur forex: poori guide, 2026 edition
The beginner's guide to Meta ads for D2C brands spending under Rs 1 lakh a month
cards.why_it_works: It signals completeness to a searcher who wants one trusted page instead of ten tabs, and the year signals freshness. The pattern is sourced from instances only (Farnam Street's 'Feynman Technique: The Ultimate Guide...'); no study of its performance was found, so treat it as a positioning label, not a proven lift.
cards.risk: Broken promise when the 'ultimate' guide is thin, outdated or written to rank rather than help. Search line: Google's spam policies target generating many pages 'for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users', whether AI or humans made them (comp:google_search_spam_policies, trend:scaled_ai_content_enforcement). In an ad, 'the only guide you'll ever need' is a claim that needs substantiation (comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022).

cards.name: Urgency / deadline
cards.summary: Tie the read or the action to a real date, quantity or window: 'Before [date]...', 'Last [N] seats'. A good one uses deadlines that exist outside the ad (tax dates, festival dates, real stock, a batch start), names the exact day and time, and the offer really ends when it says.
use_for: closing emails for sales, launches and cohorts
festival campaigns ('Diwali se pehle delivery')
tax and compliance reminders
event and webinar registrations with real capacity
limited stock drops
avoid: Countdown timers that reset on reload, or 'last chance' every week: once readers catch it, every future deadline is ignored.
Vague 'Hurry, limited time!': give the date and time ('ends Monday 11:59 pm').
Pressure on considered purchases (home loans, insurance, admissions): lead with clarity and let the real date sit in the body.
Fear-based urgency ('before it's too late for your family'): name the concrete deadline instead.
templates: [Offer] ends [day, time]. From [next day] it's [new terms].
examples: Diwali se pehle delivery chahiye? Order 24 October tak kar do.
Sunday batch: 6 seats left. Registrations close Friday 8 pm.
Our Rs 499 launch price ends Monday midnight. From Tuesday it's Rs 799.
Before your ITR due date: the 4-document checklist to finish this weekend.
cards.why_it_works: A real deadline removes the reader's default option, which is 'later'. 'Urgent' is one of the 4 Us of a headline (fw:four_us); Caples' benefit headlines include warnings against delaying a purchase (Lofgren's summary); TrueFan describes festival FOMO (do this before Diwali) as the India seasonal form.
cards.risk: Fake urgency is the line, and in India it is a legal one: fake scarcity or popularity and fake time-limited sales are a banned dark pattern; the gazette's own illustration is 'Only 2 rooms left! 30 others are looking at this right now' (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023). Coaching ads may not use false urgency (cl. 3(e), comp:ccpa_coaching_ads_2024). The UK bans false 'limited time' claims outright (comp:uk_dmcc_schedule20). Google Ads bans using negative life events to pressure immediate action (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation). Use tech:ethical_urgency.

cards.name: 'Who else wants...' headline
cards.summary: 'Who else wants [desired result]?' presupposes that many people already have the result and invites the reader to join them. It works when the result is concrete and the crowd is real, and it reads most naturally in long-form sales letters and email, where a classic direct-response voice fits.
use_for: sales-letter and long-form landing-page headlines
email subject lines for a list used to direct-response style
print ads for traditional audiences
webinar and workshop invitations
a playful Hinglish nod in reels ('Aur kisko chahiye...?')
avoid: Modern social feeds in English: the phrasing reads as vintage ad copy; use hook:social_proof with a real number, or the Hinglish 'Aur kisko chahiye...?'.
Vague results ('Who else wants success?'): name the outcome a reader can picture ('their Sundays back from bookkeeping').
Implying a crowd that does not exist: if almost no one has it yet, use hook:news_announcement instead.
Body-image versions ('Who else wants a flat stomach?'): these break Meta's health rules; lead with the product.
examples: Who else wants their Sundays back from bookkeeping?
Who else in Koramangala wants fresh idli batter delivered by 7 am?
Aur kisko chahiye 10 minute mein ready hone wala office lunch?
Who else wants a GST return filed without a single CA visit?
cards.why_it_works: The word 'else' presupposes others already have the result, so social proof and desire land in five words. Caples lists 'Who else' as a keyword opener (Lofgren's summary) and Copyblogger includes 'Who else wants [blank]?' among its 22 formulas.
cards.risk: The implied popularity must be real; a presupposed crowd that does not exist is a misleading claim, and fake popularity is a banned dark pattern in India (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023). Body and weight versions hit Meta's ban on 'statements of inferiority about physical appearance' and its 18+ targeting rule for weight-loss ads (comp:meta_advertising_standards).

cards.name: Direct 'you' address
cards.summary: Speak to the reader as 'you' about their own situation: 'Are you still [X]?', 'Your [thing] is [problem]'. A good one makes the 'you' specific (what they do, where, when), keeps the focus on the reader's world rather than the brand's, and in Hindi picks aap or tum on purpose.
use_for: ad headlines and landing-page heroes
email subject lines and first lines
reels spoken to camera
first line of a LinkedIn post
push notifications and WhatsApp messages
avoid: 'You' plus a personal attribute in Meta ads ('Are you bankrupt?', 'Your diabetes...'): Meta disallows it; talk about the product or the situation ('Sugar-free mithai for Diwali').
Accusing 'you' on sensitive topics ('You're failing your kids'): use 'most parents' or 'we'.
Mixing aap and tum, or using tum for elders and customers: aap for customers and formal brands, tum for young peer-to-peer content, and keep it consistent.
A 'you' line that fits everyone ('You deserve the best'): add the situation that makes it theirs.
examples: Your invoice is why clients pay late. Look at line 3.
Aapka WhatsApp catalogue customer ko confuse kar raha hai. Ye 3 badlav karo.
You check your Shopify dashboard 20 times a day. Only one number on it matters.
Are you still sending GST bills as photos on WhatsApp?
cards.why_it_works: Second person turns copy into a conversation with one reader, so they test the line against their own life. Caples' benefit headlines include ones where the advertiser speaks directly to the reader (Lofgren's summary), and Copyblogger's formulas use 'you' forms throughout. The full-piece habit is tech:you_focus.
cards.risk: Tips into manipulation when 'you' is used to frighten ('Your family is unprotected if you die tomorrow') or to fake an alert ('Your account will be blocked'). Legal line: Meta ads must not assert or imply personal attributes, and 'you/your' is fine only without one (comp:meta_advertising_standards); Google Ads bans using negative life events such as death, illness, arrests or bankruptcy to pressure immediate action, and ads that mimic system notifications (comp:google_ads_misrepresentation).
